passage: Sunday: At the family lunch, Uncle said loudly that people from the next district were not to be trusted. Zubin's parents nodded. So did his aunt. Zubin's stomach twisted, because his best friend Aman was from there. He looked at his plate and said nothing. His cousin Afreen caught his eye and gave a tiny shrug. Monday: at school Zubin passed Aman the ball first, on purpose, and sat next to him. Thursday: Zubin found his grandfather feeding the sparrows. "Dada, why did Uncle say those things?" Dada sighed. "He was cheated once, long ago, and it stuck." Zubin thought about that. "But Aman never cheated anybody," he said. Dada didn't answer, only looked at the sparrows.

qa.q: Who caught Zubin's eye at the family lunch?
Why did Zubin's stomach twist when Uncle spoke?
qa.a: He felt uneasy because his best friend Aman came from the next district, and Uncle's words did not match what he knew of Aman.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that let him hold his own view without a fight?
qa.a: He stayed quietly friendly with Aman at school and later asked his trusted grandfather why Uncle thinks that way.

qa.q: How might Zubin's grandfather see Uncle's opinion?
qa.a: As something that grew from one old bad experience that stuck, rather than something based on everyone from there.

grounding: A child feels uneasy when an elder talks badly about a group and the family nods, and quietly holds his own view before asking a trusted elder.

passage:
At Midsummer lunch in Grandma's garden outside Uppsala, Uncle Lars put down his fork and started one of his speeches. "People from those countries just come here for handouts. They don't want to work." A few adults nodded. Someone passed the potatoes.
Astrid's stomach turned. Her best friend Tuan's parents ran the bakery on her street and were up at four every morning. She said nothing, but she didn't nod either. She stared at her plate.
After lunch, while the others played croquet, she helped Grandma carry cups inside. "Grandma, why does Uncle Lars think that?"
Grandma sighed and dried her hands. "I think he's scared about his own job, and it's easier to blame strangers. You're right to wonder. What do you think?"
"I think he doesn't know Tuan's family."
"Then maybe one day you can tell him about them," Grandma said.

qa.q: Why did Astrid's stomach turn at the lunch?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and upset, because Uncle Lars's words did not match the hard-working family she knew.

qa.q: What did Astrid do instead of arguing at the table?
qa.a: She quietly did not nod, then asked Grandma in private why Uncle Lars thought that.

qa.q: Why might Uncle Lars talk this way, according to Grandma?
qa.a: He may be scared about his own job and find it easier to blame strangers.

grounding: A girl uneasy when an older relative speaks badly about a group quietly holds her own view and later asks a trusted elder why.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Noor sat between her Phuphi and her cousin Hafsa. When a nurse called the next name, Phuphi leaned over and whispered loudly, "Look, one of those people. Their kind are never clean. I hope she doesn't touch me." Hafsa nodded as if it were ordinary.
Noor looked at the nurse. She had gentle hands and had just helped an old man with his walking stick. Noor's stomach went tight. She didn't nod.
That night she sat by Nani. "Nani, why does Phuphi talk like that about some people?"
Nani said, "Some grown-ups learned those ideas when they were small and never questioned them. It is not right. You can keep your own view, and be kind to everyone."
Next visit, Noor decided, she would smile at that nurse.

qa.q: What had the nurse just helped an old man with?
How did Noor feel when Phuphi whispered about the nurse?
qa.a: Uneasy and uncomfortable; her stomach went tight because the words did not match what she saw.

qa.q: How did Noor hold her own view without a fight?
qa.a: She did not nod along, then later asked Nani, a trusted elder, why Phuphi talks that way.

qa.q: How might the nurse feel if she overheard Phuphi?
qa.a: Hurt and insulted, especially while she was caring for patients.

grounding: A girl uneasy when an older relative runs down a group quietly keeps her own view and later asks a trusted elder why they think so.
